svg.title: CE, PE and P: who knows what, and the three isolation boundaries in an L3VPN
svg.desc: Topology of CE1, PE1, two P routers, PE2, CE2 with a table underneath naming what each role holds. The CE exchanges routes and has no VRF at all. The PE holds VRFs, exchanges VPN routes and pushes and pops labels. The P router switches transport labels only and never sees a customer route. A right-hand panel lists the three isolation boundaries: on the CE side by physical interface or subinterface, on the PE side by VRF and route target, and in the P network by nothing at all, since P routers do not know VRFs exist. A closing note says routing policy, ACLs and QoS classification must all be completed at the PE boundary, because inside the core there is nothing of the customer to anchor on.
svg.text: Three roles, three levels of knowledge — and the isolation only happens at one of them
If you remember one thing: the P router has never heard of your VPN
CE1
PE1
P1
P2
PE2
CE2
route
label
swap
swap
pop
CE — customer edge
Has no VRF at all. Exchanges routes
with the PE and knows nothing about
labels, RTs or the provider core.
PE — provider edge (the only device that matters)
Holds one VRF per customer per site, exchanges VPNv4
routes with other PEs, and pushes or pops both labels.
All policy lives here, because it is the last place it can.
P — provider node
Swaps transport labels only. Holds no
VPN routes and does not know VRFs
exist. Cheapest, fastest, blindest.
WHERE ISOLATION ACTUALLY COMES FROM
CE side: physical interface or subinterface, or VRF-Lite on the CE itself.
PE side: VRF plus route targets. This is the only hop where the
customer's identity is carried as a decision.
P network: nothing. Isolation is a property of the edges; the core
is deliberately ignorant, which is what makes it scale.
The consequence nobody plans for
Routing policy, ACLs and QoS classification must be finished
at the PE boundary. Once the packet is inside the core there is
no customer anchor left: the P router cannot match on your
prefixes, your VRFs or your applications.
Design check: for every policy you intend to enforce, name the device that executes it. If the answer is “the core”, the policy does not exist.
This is also why a carrier-managed PE is a governance decision, not a technical one: whoever owns the PE owns your policy point.
Troubleshooting order: CE routing table (did the route arrive) → PE VRF table (did the RT match) → VPNv4 table (was it advertised) → LFIB (is there a label path).
